summary: Defines XML formats for lists of resources, such as users, that a single URI can stand for. For instance, when a SIP SUBSCRIBE targets a list service, the server can expand the list and subscribe to each member.

eli5.summary: One name can stand for a whole group. This defines the XML for writing such a group list, so a request for the group reaches everyone in it.

questions: what is a sip resource list
what is an rls services document
how does a resource list server expand a list
subtitle: Two XML formats for naming groups of users and for attaching a SIP service URI to such a group.

tldr.problem: SIP services such as presence lists or conferences need a list of users or resources, and there was no standard way to write that list or to tie it to a service URI.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a resource-lists XML document that holds lists of entries, and an rls-services XML document that maps a service URI to a list and to the event packages it supports. Both can be managed with XCAP.
tldr.outcome: A resource list server can take a SUBSCRIBE to a service URI, flatten the referenced list into URIs and subscribe to each. The lists can also be reused by other applications.

today: RFC 4826 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata for this RFC lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It depends on XCAP (RFC 4825) and on the resource list SUBSCRIBE extension in RFC 4662.

sections.title: Lists Behind a Single URI
sections.content:
A SIP URI can name a person such as sip:joe@example.com, but it can also name a service such as voicemail, conferencing or a presence list. Such a service needs a list of users, or more generally resources. When a SIP request arrives at the service URI, the server reads the list and performs an operation against each member.

Examples in the RFC are a presence list service, where a SUBSCRIBE asks for presence of every user on a list, and an instant conference service, where an INVITE creates a call with the group. A presence list server is a specific case of a resource list server (RLS).

Keeping the list separate from the service is useful. A client could store a list on disk or email it to friends, so a standard format is needed. The RFC therefore defines two XML documents and an XCAP application usage for each.
sections.eli5: One special name can stand for a whole group of people. To make that work, you need a written list of the group and a note saying which name uses it.

sections.title: The Resource Lists Document
sections.content:
A resource lists document is XML 1.0, MUST be well-formed and valid, and MUST be encoded in UTF-8. Its namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:resource-lists. The root element <resource-lists> holds zero or more <list> elements.

A <list> may have a name attribute, which must be unique among sibling lists, and an optional <display-name>. It contains <entry>, nested <list>, <entry-ref> and <external> elements, so lists can be hierarchical.

  • <entry> has a mandatory uri attribute naming one resource. The format does not restrict the URI type, though an RLS needs subscribeable ones such as SIP and pres URIs. Uniqueness among siblings is by case-sensitive string comparison.
  • <entry-ref> has a mandatory ref attribute, a relative path reference to an entry in the same XCAP root, included by reference instead of by value.
  • <external> has an anchor attribute, an absolute HTTP URI of a whole list that may live on another server.

Entry-ref and external elements only make sense in documents obtained from an XCAP server. The XCAP server does not resolve them. The entity using the document, for example the client or the RLS, must do so.
sections.eli5: A list is a folder of names. A name can be written right in the folder, or the folder can say 'see the name on that other page', or 'use the whole list over at that other office'.

sections.title: Managing Lists with XCAP
sections.content:
Resource lists can be edited with XCAP. The RFC defines the resource-lists application unique ID, the MIME type application/resource-lists+xml and the default namespace. It leaves the default XCAP authorization policy unchanged: only a user can read, write or modify their own documents.

Because uniqueness is checked by case-sensitive string comparison, two URIs that are equal under their scheme's rules might differ as strings. A client that is unsure whether it is creating or replacing an element SHOULD canonicalize the URI first. For HTTP URIs the basic algorithm removes the default port (80), lowercases the hostname and removes unnecessary percent-encoding.

The XCAP server enforces uniqueness of name, uri, ref and anchor values within a parent. It is not responsible for checking that references actually resolve, since a reference to another domain cannot be guaranteed without substantial complexity.
sections.eli5: People edit their lists through a shared filing cabinet. The cabinet makes sure no two names in a folder are spelled identically, but it does not check that every pointer to another page leads somewhere real.

sections.title: The RLS Services Document
sections.content:
An RLS services document defines URIs that stand for services at a resource list server. Its namespace is urn:ietf:params:xml:ns:rls-services and its root is <rls-services>, holding <service> elements.

Each <service> has a mandatory uri attribute: subscribing to that URI gives the service. Its children name the list in one of two ways. A <list> element includes the list directly, so one XCAP operation creates list and members, but the list is then hidden inside the service and unusable by other applications. A <resource-list> element holds an absolute HTTP URI pointing to a <list> in a resource-lists document, so the list can be reused.

An optional <packages> element holds <package> elements naming the SIP event packages the service supports. When it is absent, the service accepts subscriptions for any event package.
sections.eli5: This second document is the phone book entry. It says 'this special number uses that roster, and it answers these kinds of questions'.

sections.title: Global Index and Service Lookup
sections.content:
A service uri must be unique across all <service> elements on a server, across XCAP roots, and must not match an existing resource in the URI's domain. A violating request MUST be rejected with a 409, and the server can suggest unused alternatives. A client wanting a vanity URI can just try it, and retry on a <uniqueness-failure> conflict.

To help the RLS find a service, the XCAP server keeps one document named index in the global tree. It is the union of all <service> elements from every user document named index in the same XCAP root. So clients SHOULD define services in the user document named index, or the service will not be picked up. The server need not store the global document and may build responses dynamically. Access to it MUST be restricted to trusted elements in the server's domain, because it holds information about all users.
sections.eli5: The cabinet also keeps one big master index of every special number, so the group-calling machine can find the right entry fast. Only the trusted machine is allowed to read that index.

sections.title: How an RLS Expands a List
sections.content:
On a SUBSCRIBE, the RLS finds the <service> whose uri matches the Request URI. One suggested approach is to canonicalize the URI and do an XCAP GET against the global index. If <packages> is present and the requested event package is not listed, the request MUST be rejected with 489 (Bad Event). Otherwise it SHOULD be processed, after authorizing the subscriber.

The RLS then builds a flat list of URIs by walking the tree under the list, in any order such as depth-first or breadth-first. It keeps a flat list and a traversed list of external URIs already visited.

  • <entry>: add its uri to the flat list if not already present and the scheme can service subscriptions.
  • <entry-ref>: resolve the relative reference against the XCAP root. If the result is not a 200 OK containing an entry, the request SHOULD be rejected with 502 (Bad Gateway).
  • <external>: if its anchor is already on the traversed list, the server MUST stop traversing and SHOULD reject with 502. Otherwise it records the URI, dereferences it and substitutes the returned list.

The traversed list prevents recursive loops. Rejecting is only SHOULD strength, because in some cases an RLS may serve better by subscribing to the URIs it could obtain and omitting the rest. Finally the RLS creates a virtual subscription to each URI in the flat list.
sections.eli5: To answer, the machine reads the roster, follows every pointer, and keeps a note of the pages it has already visited so it never walks in circles. Then it knocks on each person's door.

sections.title: SIP URI Canonicalization
sections.content:
Two SIP URIs can be equal under RFC 3261 comparison rules but look different as text. The canonicalization procedure makes them match under case-sensitive string comparison in most cases.

  1. Lowercase the domain part and any tokens such as user, transport or udp.
  2. Remove percent-encoding for characters that do not need it. For example sip:%6aoe%20smith@example.com becomes sip:joe%20smith@example.com.
  3. Reorder URI parameters into lexical order by parameter name, using US-ASCII numeric values with the leftmost character most significant.
  4. Discard any header parameters.

Functionally equal URIs get equal canonical forms if neither has header parameters and, if one carries a URI parameter not defined in RFC 3261, the other does too.
sections.eli5: It is like writing every name in lowercase and sorting the details alphabetically, so 'JOE' and 'joe' end up looking identical when you compare them.

sections.title: Extensibility, Security and IANA
sections.content:
Both documents are meant to be extended by adding new elements in a new XML namespace governed by a new schema. The extension namespace MUST differ from those defined here, and an extension MUST NOT change the syntax or semantics of these schemas. Extensions MUST specify where their elements may appear.

The schemas mark the allowed places with <any> and <anyAttribute>. A document with extensions therefore needs several schemas to validate. These schemas carry no version number, since the RFC does not expect one to be needed. A revision would try to keep old documents compliant.

Both documents are particularly sensitive, because they show the set of people a user wants to communicate with. Clients SHOULD use TLS when contacting servers to fetch them, which is no change from XCAP.

IANA considerations register two XCAP application unique IDs (resource-lists and rls-services), two MIME types (application/resource-lists+xml with file extension .rl, and application/rls-services+xml with .rs), two XML namespace URNs and two schema URNs.
sections.eli5:
The forms have a few blank boxes for extra notes. You can add new kinds of notes, but you may not change what the existing boxes mean.

A list of your contacts is private, so you should send it through a locked tube rather than an open one.
